extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / policymakers interested in postwar affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on international/postwar developments (committees, military tests, medical surveys) in a mid-20th-century newspaper format. Covers mandates, findings and logistical considerations for government and military actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anglo‑American Committee terms of reference (mandate and tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. To examine political, economic and social conditions in Palestine as they bear upon the problem of Jewish immigration and settlement therein and of the peoples now living therein. 2. To examine the position of the Jews in those countries in Europe where they have been victims of Nazi and Fascist persecution, and the practical measures taken or contemplated to be taken in those countries to enable them to live free from discrimination and estimates of those who wish or will be impelled by their conditions to migrate to Palestine or other countries outside Europe. (Also: take views of competent witnesses; consult representative Arabs and Jews; make recommendations to His Majesty's government and the government of the United States for interim handling and permanent resolution.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee is to gather evidence and testimony, consult representative parties (Arabs and Jews), examine social/economic/political conditions and practical measures in Europe, and then make both interim and permanent recommendations to the British and U.S. governments. The committee was instructed to make its report within 120 days after beginning its inquiry and may operate through subcommittees and rotating chairmanships as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee timeline and operating procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anglo‑American Committee is to make its report within 120 days after it begins its inquiry; it may deal simultaneously through the medium of subcommittees with various terms of reference; the procedure of the committee will be determined by the committee itself and it will be open to deal, if it thinks fit, through subcommittees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit deadline (120 days) for the committee report is specified; the committee has procedural flexibility to form subcommittees and to extend or determine its own internal procedures. The committee is empowered to gather testimony and consult representatives and governments as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anglo‑American Committee composition and chairmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: A twelve‑member Anglo‑American committee with rotating chairmanship; U.S. and British co-chairs (American chairman Joseph C. Hutcheson, British chairman Sir John E. Singleton) and membership drawn from judges, former college presidents/academics, editors, former government officials and diplomats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition guidance implies balanced Anglo‑American representation, legal/judicial leadership, inclusion of academics and experienced public servants or policy figures. Rotating chairmanship between the two governments is specified as the operating arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postwar civil‑defense and hospital design recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations from the U.S. strategic bombing medical survey: construct hospitals with reinforced walls (example language: 'walls of reinforced ... nine feet thick'), consider tower‑like, windowless air‑raid hospitals, provide underground refuges or ground institutions as refuges; locate hospitals on the periphery of cities; plan placement and protection of food supplies for use when transportation networks are destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings about bombing effects lead to prescriptive guidance on civil‑defense infrastructure: hospitals should be robustly constructed and sited to reduce vulnerability (peripheral location, reinforced structures, underground refuge capability); food processing, storage and distribution systems must be protected and plans made for local reserves when transport is disrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings on causes and characteristics of bombing casualties (implications for shelter/survival planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medical survey found 'fire blizzards' and incendiary attacks produced extreme heat (air super‑heated to ~1,400°F), causing deaths by inhalation of super‑heated air, carbon monoxide poisoning, dehydration of bodies (mummification) and mass shelter deaths despite lack of external injuries; hospitals were razed and could not be relied upon as shields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These findings imply specific survival/shelter design considerations: standard shelters may not protect against super‑heated air or carbon monoxide; evacuation/shelter strategies must account for inhalation risks and internal heat; reliance on hospital markings or central hospitals as safe havens is unsafe — protection must be structural and redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic‑bomb at‑sea test planning considerations (Army‑Navy joint experiment logistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The planned joint Army‑Navy tests involve assembling many naval vessels, extensive instrumentation to record pressures, heat, radioactivity and other aspects of blast on and above the sea; selection of target vessels is a planning choice and patrols/measurements must be arranged; security and compartmentalization practices affect scientific progress and foreign replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational planning must cover logistics (vessel assembly, instrumentation, personnel), selection of suitable targets and patrol/observation plans, and balance between necessary security (compartmentalization) and adequate scientific communication to avoid unnecessary delays or duplication of less‑efficient methods. The Navy and Army coordinate target and measurement roles in the joint experiment.
